The sea below the town of Oakhaven had not contained water for three hundred years. Instead, it was a vast basin of crushed lapis salt that moved in slow, silent swells driven by deep winds no one could feel on land. On the third Tuesday of every month, when the twin moons lined up like pale buttons on the sky’s coat, the dry tide brought in the unspelt things.

Julian sat on the limestone ledge, his heavy boots dangling over eight hundred feet of empty air. In his lap rested a brass telescope with five nested quartz lenses. He adjusted the smallest lens with a turn of his thumb. Through the glass, the blue dust below vibrated with faint golden sparks: the dropped keys of old conversations, the scent of rain that never fell, and the names of pets forgotten before childhood ended.

Julian was a Retriever. It was not a grand profession, nor a lucrative one, but it kept oil in his lamps and fresh bread on his table. Most people lived forward, aggressively building tomorrow out of brick and ambition. Julian lived at the quiet margins, gathering offcuts of yesterday before the salt dissolved them into pure nameless light. Behind him, the heavy door to his cliffside workshop creaked open on leather hinges.

"You are late today, Julian," Martha called out, carrying a basket covered with a checked cloth. She was eighty years old; in Oakhaven, people stopped counting years once their hair turned the color of the salt floor below.

"The wind had a heavy shoulder this morning," Julian said, lowering his glass and wiping blue dust from his cuff. "Look down there—there is a whole spool of late afternoon sunlight from forty years ago floating near the spire. But salt eats numbers first. Numbers have no heart, you see. They puncture the foam and sink."

Julian stood, his knees popping in the crisp morning air, and picked up his long net of silver wire and goat hair. It was the only mesh fine enough to catch a thought without tearing it.

"A stranger came by the square this morning," Martha remarked, leaning against a worktable littered with tiny tweezers. "Asking about things that drop from the sky. She had no jars, only a silver chain around her wrist with nothing attached to it except an open clasp."

The bronze bell above the door chimed softly. Standing in the doorway framed by the harsh glare of the salt sea was a woman in a dark traveling coat. Her boots were dusted in pale violet, meaning she had taken the long path through the lower terraces.

"Are you the man who fishes in the dry?" she asked, her voice steady like silk stretched over wire. "I lost something. Taken by an hour I was not looking."

Julian motioned toward an oak stool. "Sit down. Salt dust gets into the throat near the edge. What was it?"

"A song," she said, her fingers tightening on her coat. "Four notes my mother whistled when pulling bread from the oven on cold winter mornings. I had it yesterday. I woke up today, and the space where it lived was empty
